walkthroughs.body_html:
Thermodynamics — a core area of A-Level Chemistry.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Thermodynamics brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Thermodynamics.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which species has the same electron configuration as Ar?
options: Na⁺
Cl⁻
F⁻
Mg²⁺

mcqs.q: Successive ionisation energies of an atom always:
options: Decrease
Stay the same
Increase
Vary randomly

mcqs.q: What does an increase in entropy of a system correspond to?
options: A reaction with negative delta G must be exothermic in every case.
An increase in the number of ways energy and particles can be arranged — typically a more dispersed/'disordered' state.
Entropy measures how much energy a system contains in total.
Entropy is just a measure of how messy a system looks visually.

mcqs.q: If a reaction has a negative Gibbs free energy change, what does that mean?
options: The reaction is thermodynamically feasible — it can proceed — but it may still be very slow.
A reaction with negative delta G will always happen quickly.
A reaction with negative delta G must be exothermic in every case.
Entropy measures how much energy a system contains in total.

mcqs.q: Why can an endothermic reaction still be spontaneous?
options: A reaction with negative delta G must be exothermic in every case.
Endothermic reactions are never spontaneous because they require energy input.
All endothermic reactions are spontaneous at room temperature.
If the entropy increase (TΔS) is large enough to outweigh the positive ΔH, ΔG can still be negative.
